newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: Dawn and dusk shelling becomes Congo pattern.
newsitem.headline: Dawn and dusk shelling becomes Congo pattern.

text.p: Congo's capital Brazzaville suffered fresh shelling on Tuesday as a conflict between the president and a rival took on a pattern of dawn and dusk skirmishes.
Mortar fire disturbed the calm at about 6 a.m. (0500 GMT) on Tuesday after a round of shelling early on Monday evening.
"It's often like this between the hours of six and seven," said one foreign resident who has stayed put throughout a month of heavy fighting and only relatively peaceful truces.

President Pascal Lissouba left the city on Monday for the first time since the clashes began, flying to national day festivities across the river in Kinshasa in Laurent Kabila's Democratic Republic of the Congo.

He returned in the afternoon after a visit that diplomats said served to show he held the city airport and felt confident enough to be absent from his beleaguered capital, parts of which his rival Denis Sassou Nguesso controls.
French ambassador Raymond Cesaire said on Monday that fighting had broken out near his embassy in the deserted city centre.

"It seems to involve battles between bands of looters or soldiers letting off steam, rather than a threat or a deliberate break of the ceasefire by one side or the other," he told Reuters by telephone.
More serious battles died down on Friday ahead of a new ceasefire between Lissouba and Sassou.
Brazzaville has been devastated by shelling, street battles and looting since June 5.
Aid workers estimate 1,000 to 3,000 people, mostly civilians, have died. Some of the heaviest fighting has been for the city airport.
A lasting political solution seems no nearer.
Both Lissouba and Sassou say they want free and fair presidential elections, but disagree on how to hold them.

International mediation efforts led by Omar Bongo, president of neighbouring Gabon, have centred on the dispatch of an African intervention force but the United Nations says there must be a lasting peace first.
